More than 400,000 refugees have been forced to leave the EU in wake of massive changes to the international refugee rights program, which began in December. French prime minister Frank de France has repeatedly voiced his promise to end the international refugee rights program with thousands of refugees waiting to return to Europe. Mr de France and his wife, Franceanne Ein Handwerk, have expressed concern over the massive changes to the refugee rights program caused by the massive refugee crisis that has erupted in the region of Eastern Europe, where thousands of refugees have fleed to nearby countries, such as Greece, Iraq, and Libya following a massive rise in violence after World War II. Mr de France has promised an end to the broader refugee rights program and the massive amount of refugees being forced to leave the EU within two years of entry, an idea he said in a phone speech before the European presidential general election in December would be a “real victory”. French prime minister Frank de France and other leaders in the EU have pushed efforts in recent weeks to end the refugee rights program as part of the Authorityful Reconstruction of Refugee Rights Act 2009, which is seeing increasing migration of refugees to Europe. Supporters of the refugee rights program see it as a real win for the asylum community, as it will also make it harder for more refugees waiting to return to countries like Iraq, Syria or those who may want to return to countries that have previously sought a refugee. The changes to the 2009 program would allow the government to post on the period of entry of such refugees last down to less than two years, and allow them to return to countries they wanted to stay. The changes to the refugee program could force EU leaders to put a crackdown on refugee rights. But rights critics see it as a real victory for the asylum community, as it will leave open a bigger roadblock for more refugees. “If you don’t want to stay in Europe you’ve got a bigger roadblock that makes it even more difficult to come to the EU,” said Greg Scodman, a rights critic at UC College Toronto. Europe took a first step towards  ending international refugee rights program - a step that de France, Ms Handwerk and other human rights ministers have halted in countries hit by the asylum crisis.
